questions.stem: In psychology, the mind-body problem is the question of:
options: whether the brain or the spinal cord controls reflex actions
how the left and right hemispheres share out mental tasks
whether physical illness is more harmful than mental illness
how mental experience relates to the physical brain and body
questions.explanation: The mind-body problem asks whether the mind is something separate from the physical body or is produced by it, and how the two are related. Questions about reflexes or hemispheres are about brain function, not about the nature of the mind itself.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the materialist approach to the mind-body problem?
options: The mind is a product of the physical activity of the brain
The mind is a non-physical substance separate from the body
The mind is located in the heart and controlled by the blood
The mind and body are separate but interact in the cerebellum
questions.explanation: Materialism holds that mental processes are physical processes of the brain, so there is no separate non-physical mind. The view that the mind is a separate non-physical substance is dualism, the position associated with Descartes.

questions.stem: The Roman-era physician Claudius Galen is linked to the materialist approach. Which of his ideas fits that approach?
options: The pineal gland is the point where a non-physical mind meets the body
Mental functions depend on the brain, as shown by dissecting and injuring animals
The mind is a soul that exists apart from the body and survives its death
Character can be read from the shape of bumps on the outside of the skull
questions.explanation: Galen dissected animals and observed that damage to the brain and nerves affected movement and sensation, so he placed mental functions in the physical brain. Reading the skull is phrenology, from Gall, and the pineal gland as a meeting point is Descartes' dualism.

questions.stem: Rene Descartes argued that the body is like a machine but the mind is not. Why is his view called dualism?
options: He treated the mind and body as two different kinds of thing
He divided the brain into two hemispheres with separate roles
He claimed that every thought has both a cause and an effect
He said the nervous system has two divisions, central and peripheral
questions.explanation: Dualism means the mind and body are two distinct entities: a non-physical mind that thinks, and a physical body that works mechanically. The term does not refer to the two hemispheres or the divisions of the nervous system.

questions.stem: A modern neuroscientist shows that a person's mood changes in predictable ways when a drug alters chemical activity in their brain. Which approach does this evidence most directly support?
options: The materialist approach, because a physical change produced a mental change
The dualist approach, because the mind responded separately from the brain
The phrenological approach, because one trait was linked to one brain area
The dualist approach, because the drug acted on the pineal gland alone
questions.explanation: If altering brain chemistry reliably changes a mental state, mental states appear to depend on physical brain processes, which is the materialist position. Dualism would predict some independence between the mind and brain, and nothing here involves skull shape or the pineal gland.

questions.stem: Franz Gall's phrenology was based on the assumption that:
options: the brain works as a whole, so damage anywhere has the same general effect
electrical stimulation of the cortex can trigger memories and movements
a non-physical mind controls the body through a small gland in the brain
a well-used mental faculty enlarges its brain area and so bulges the skull
questions.explanation: Gall proposed that the brain is made of separate organs for faculties such as kindness or pride, and that a stronger faculty enlarged its organ and pushed out the skull above it. The idea that the brain works as a whole came from Flourens, partly in response to phrenology.

questions.stem: Phrenology has been rejected, yet it is often credited with influencing later brain research. Which idea did it help introduce?
options: That brain tissue carries messages as electrical impulses along nerve fibres
That different mental functions may be localised in different parts of the brain
That the skull's shape reliably reveals a person's intelligence and personality
That the mind is a non-physical substance that has no location in the body
questions.explanation: Phrenology's specific claims about skull bumps were wrong, but its central idea that functions are localised in particular brain areas was later supported by research such as Broca's. Reading the skull for traits is exactly the part that was discredited.

questions.stem: Pierre Flourens studied the brain by:
options: removing parts of the brains of animals and observing the effects
measuring bumps on the skulls of people with known personalities
stimulating the cortex of conscious human patients during surgery
recording electrical activity through electrodes on the scalp
questions.explanation: In the early 1800s Flourens used ablation, surgically removing brain areas in animals such as pigeons and rabbits and observing the changes in behaviour. Stimulating the cortex of conscious patients is the later method of Wilder Penfield.

questions.stem: Flourens removed the cerebellum of animals and found they could still move but their movements became uncoordinated. What did he conclude?
options: The cerebellum is involved in coordinating movement
The cerebellum is the starting point of all voluntary movement
The cerebellum controls breathing and heart rate
The cerebellum stores memories of learned movements
questions.explanation: Because movement continued but lost its coordination, Flourens concluded that the cerebellum coordinates movement rather than starting it. Vital functions such as breathing and heart rate he linked to the medulla, which is why damage there was fatal.

questions.stem: Flourens found that removing different parts of the cerebral cortex of animals produced similar general losses rather than the loss of specific abilities. How did this finding relate to phrenology?
options: It supported phrenology's claim that each faculty is located in a particular cortical area
It challenged phrenology's claim that the mind is produced by the physical brain
It challenged phrenology's claim that the cortex has separate areas for separate faculties
It supported phrenology's claim that the skull's shape matches the size of brain areas
questions.explanation: Phrenology claimed the cortex was a set of separate organs for separate faculties. Flourens' finding that the cortex seemed to work as a whole contradicted this. Both Gall and Flourens placed the mind in the brain, so that was not the point of disagreement.

questions.stem: During surgery for epilepsy, Wilder Penfield electrically stimulated the cortex of patients who were awake. Why could the patients stay conscious?
options: The brain itself has no pain receptors, so only the scalp needed local anaesthetic
Electrical stimulation blocks all pain signals travelling to the brain
The patients were given a drug that removed all sensation from the body
Only the spinal cord detects pain, so the brain could be touched freely
questions.explanation: Brain tissue has no pain receptors, so with local anaesthetic for the scalp and skull, patients could stay awake and report what they experienced when each area was stimulated. Pain is still detected elsewhere in the body; the brain simply cannot feel being touched.

questions.stem: When Penfield stimulated a strip of cortex, his patients' hands or legs twitched, and stimulating nearby points moved neighbouring body parts. What did this allow him to do?
options: Show that every part of the cortex controls movement equally
Show that movement is controlled only by the cerebellum
Map the bumps on the skull that match particular traits
Map which areas of the cortex control movement of particular body parts
questions.explanation: By recording which body part responded to stimulation at each point, Penfield mapped the motor cortex and, with patients' reports of sensations, the somatosensory cortex. This supported localisation of function, the opposite of every area doing the same thing.

questions.stem: Knowledge of the brain has historically come at the cost of risky and invasive practices. Which method is the clearest example?
options: Asking participants to keep a diary of their thoughts and feelings
Removing brain tissue from animals to observe changes in behaviour
Recording electrical activity from the scalp with surface electrodes
Scanning the brain with strong magnetic fields and radio waves
questions.explanation: Ablation destroys brain tissue permanently, so it is highly invasive and is why early research relied on animals. EEG and MRI are non-invasive, and modern imaging has reduced the need for risky procedures.

questions.stem: Which neuroimaging technique uses a radioactive tracer injected into the bloodstream to show areas of high brain activity?
options: electroencephalography (EEG)
functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)
positron emission tomography (PET)
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
questions.explanation: In a PET scan, a radioactive tracer such as glucose is taken up most by the most active brain areas, and the scanner detects the radiation it gives off. MRI and fMRI use magnetic fields and radio waves, with no radioactive substance.

questions.stem: What does an MRI scan of the brain mainly provide?
options: An image of changes in blood oxygen during tasks
A measure of how much glucose the brain uses
A detailed image of the brain's structure
A recording of electrical activity over time
questions.explanation: Standard MRI uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to produce detailed pictures of brain structure, such as a tumour or damaged area. It does not show activity; that needs fMRI, PET or EEG.

questions.stem: fMRI detects brain activity indirectly. What does it actually measure?
options: Changes in the level of oxygenated blood flowing to brain areas
Changes in the electrical charge of neurons near the scalp
Radiation given off by a tracer that active neurons absorb
Changes in the size of brain structures during a task
questions.explanation: Active neurons use more oxygen, so oxygen-rich blood flows to them, and fMRI detects the change in blood oxygen level. Electrical activity at the scalp is what EEG records, and a radioactive tracer is used in PET.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to record the exact moment, to within milliseconds, that the brain responds to a sudden sound. Which technique is most suitable?
options: fMRI, because it shows the precise location of activity
MRI, because it gives the most detailed image of the brain
PET, because it shows which areas use the most glucose
EEG, because it records electrical activity as it happens
questions.explanation: EEG records the brain's electrical activity directly, so it tracks changes in milliseconds. fMRI has better spatial detail but depends on blood flow, which lags seconds behind neural activity, and MRI shows only structure.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares EEG and fMRI?
options: Both show brain structure in detail, but only fMRI exposes people to radiation
Both record electrical activity, but fMRI records it from deeper brain areas
EEG is better at showing when activity occurs; fMRI is better at showing where
EEG is better at showing where activity occurs; fMRI is better at showing when
questions.explanation: EEG has excellent temporal resolution but poor spatial resolution, because scalp electrodes pick up activity from broad regions. fMRI pinpoints areas precisely but is slower, since blood flow changes take seconds. Neither uses radiation; that is PET.

questions.stem: Researchers compare the brains of people with and without a memory disorder. They first need to measure the size of the hippocampus, then find which areas are active while participants learn word lists. Which pair of techniques fits best?
options: PET to measure the hippocampus, then MRI to find active areas
MRI to measure the hippocampus, then fMRI to find active areas
EEG to measure the hippocampus, then MRI to find active areas
fMRI to measure the hippocampus, then EEG to find active areas
questions.explanation: MRI gives detailed structural images, so it can measure the size of a structure. fMRI then shows which areas become more active during learning, with good spatial detail. MRI alone shows no activity, and EEG cannot locate deep structures precisely.

questions.stem: The central nervous system consists of:
options: the somatic and autonomic nervous systems
the spinal cord and all sensory neurons
the brain and the spinal cord
the brain and the cranial nerves
questions.explanation: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord, which process information and coordinate responses. The somatic and autonomic nervous systems are the two divisions of the peripheral nervous system.

questions.stem: Which division of the nervous system controls heart rate, digestion and other bodily functions that occur without conscious effort?
options: the sensory nervous system
the autonomic nervous system
the somatic nervous system
the central nervous system
questions.explanation: The autonomic nervous system, part of the peripheral nervous system, regulates internal organs and glands largely automatically. The somatic nervous system carries sensory information and controls voluntary movement of skeletal muscles.

questions.stem: Priya decides to pick up a pencil and does so. Which division of the peripheral nervous system carries the messages from her brain to the muscles of her hand?
options: the central nervous system
the parasympathetic nervous system
the somatic nervous system
the autonomic nervous system
questions.explanation: Voluntary movement of skeletal muscles is controlled through the somatic nervous system, which carries motor messages from the central nervous system to the muscles. The autonomic system, including the parasympathetic division, controls internal organs and glands.

questions.stem: Which part of a neuron receives messages from other neurons?
options: the axon terminals
the myelin sheath
the axon
the dendrites
questions.explanation: Dendrites are branching extensions that receive signals from other neurons and pass them to the cell body. Axon terminals are at the other end and release neurotransmitter to the next cell.

questions.stem: What is the function of the myelin sheath?
options: It receives chemical messages from neighbouring neurons
It contains the nucleus and keeps the neuron alive
It releases neurotransmitter into the gap between neurons
It insulates the axon and speeds up the transmission of impulses
questions.explanation: The myelin sheath is a fatty layer around many axons that insulates them, so impulses travel much faster. Receiving messages is the role of the dendrites, and the cell body contains the nucleus.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the path of a neural impulse through a single neuron?
options: cell body, dendrites, axon terminals, axon
dendrites, axon, cell body, axon terminals
dendrites, cell body, axon, axon terminals
axon terminals, axon, cell body, dendrites
questions.explanation: Messages are received by the dendrites, pass to the cell body, travel down the axon, and reach the axon terminals, where neurotransmitter is released to the next cell. The impulse travels in one direction only.

questions.stem: Which type of neuron is found only within the central nervous system and connects sensory and motor neurons?
options: sensory neurons
motor neurons
afferent neurons
interneurons
questions.explanation: Interneurons lie within the brain and spinal cord and relay messages between sensory and motor neurons, as in a spinal reflex. Sensory neurons, also called afferent neurons, carry messages from receptors towards the central nervous system.

questions.stem: Tom steps on a sharp shell and his leg lifts before he is aware of pain. Which statement correctly contrasts the neurons involved?
options: Interneurons carry the message in, sensory neurons relay it, motor neurons carry it out
Sensory neurons carry the message in, interneurons relay it, motor neurons carry it out
Motor neurons carry the message in, interneurons relay it, sensory neurons carry it out
Sensory neurons carry the message in, motor neurons relay it, interneurons carry it out
questions.explanation: Sensory (afferent) neurons carry the message from receptors in the foot to the spinal cord, interneurons there pass it on, and motor (efferent) neurons carry the message out to the leg muscles. This is a reflex, so the movement begins before the brain registers pain.

questions.stem: Which structures make up the hindbrain?
options: the thalamus, hypothalamus and cortex
the medulla, thalamus and amygdala
the pons, hypothalamus and cerebellum
the medulla, pons and cerebellum
questions.explanation: The hindbrain, at the base of the brain, includes the medulla, the pons and the cerebellum. The thalamus, hypothalamus and cerebral cortex are all parts of the forebrain.

questions.stem: A drug overdose damages the medulla. Why is this life-threatening?
options: The medulla controls vital functions such as breathing and heart rate
The medulla relays all sensory information to the cerebral cortex
The medulla coordinates balance and smooth voluntary movement
The medulla regulates hunger, thirst and body temperature
questions.explanation: The medulla, in the hindbrain, controls automatic vital functions such as breathing, heart rate and blood pressure, so damage can stop them. Relaying sensory information is the role of the thalamus, and balance and coordination belong to the cerebellum.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the midbrain?
options: It sits below the thalamus and controls hunger, thirst and body temperature
It connects the hindbrain and forebrain and helps with orienting to sights and sounds
It is the largest part of the brain and is responsible for thinking and language
It lies at the back of the brain and coordinates balance and fine movement
questions.explanation: The midbrain lies between the hindbrain and forebrain. It passes information between them and has areas involved in reflexive responses to visual and auditory stimuli, such as turning towards a sudden noise. Thinking and language depend on the forebrain's cortex.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain contains the cerebral cortex, thalamus and hypothalamus?
options: the hindbrain
the brainstem
the forebrain
the midbrain
questions.explanation: The forebrain is the largest and most recently evolved region, and includes the cerebral cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus and limbic structures. It supports complex processes such as thinking, language and planning.

questions.stem: After a head injury, Mara can think, speak and remember normally, but she sways when she stands and cannot touch her nose smoothly with her finger. Which region of the brain is most likely damaged?
options: the spinal cord
the hindbrain
the forebrain
the midbrain
questions.explanation: Problems with balance and smooth, coordinated movement point to the cerebellum, which is part of the hindbrain. Her thinking, speech and memory are normal, which suggests the forebrain's cortex is not the damaged region.

questions.stem: Broca's area, usually in the left frontal lobe, is mainly involved in:
options: hearing sounds and recognising their pitch
seeing written words and recognising letters
producing fluent, articulate speech
understanding spoken and written language
questions.explanation: Broca's area plans and coordinates the movements needed to produce speech. Understanding language depends mainly on Wernicke's area in the left temporal lobe.

questions.stem: After a stroke, Hamish understands what people say to him, but his own speech is slow and effortful, with many words left out. Which area is most likely damaged?
options: the occipital lobe
Broca's area
Wernicke's area
Geschwind's territory
questions.explanation: Slow, halting speech with good understanding is the pattern of Broca's aphasia, caused by damage to Broca's area. Damage to Wernicke's area gives the opposite pattern: fluent speech that makes little sense and poor comprehension.

questions.stem: Where is Geschwind's territory, and why is it important for language?
options: In the frontal lobe, sending motor messages to the muscles of the mouth and tongue
In the temporal lobe, detecting the pitch and loudness of incoming speech sounds
In the parietal lobe, linking Wernicke's and Broca's areas to integrate word meaning
In the occipital lobe, receiving visual images of letters and words from the eyes
questions.explanation: Geschwind's territory, in the inferior parietal lobe, is connected to both Broca's and Wernicke's areas and is thought to integrate auditory, visual and other information about words, such as linking a written word to its sound and meaning. Speech movements are controlled from the frontal lobe.

questions.stem: Asha reads a word aloud. Which sequence best describes the interacting roles of the language areas involved?
options: Wernicke's area, visual cortex, Broca's area, Geschwind's territory, motor cortex
Visual cortex, Geschwind's territory, Wernicke's area, Broca's area, motor cortex
Visual cortex, Broca's area, Wernicke's area, Geschwind's territory, motor cortex
Motor cortex, Broca's area, Wernicke's area, Geschwind's territory, visual cortex
questions.explanation: The visual cortex sees the word, Geschwind's territory links its visual form to its sound, Wernicke's area gives it meaning, and Broca's area plans the speech that the motor cortex then carries out. Broca's area comes late in the sequence because it prepares the spoken output.

questions.stem: Knowing the roles of brain areas lets psychologists predict the effects of damage. A stroke damages Wernicke's area but leaves Broca's area intact. Which prediction is most accurate?
options: Speech and comprehension will both be normal, but reading aloud will be impossible
Speech will stop entirely, but comprehension of written words will stay intact
Speech will flow easily but will make little sense, and comprehension will be poor
Speech will be slow and effortful, but comprehension will stay mostly intact
questions.explanation: With Broca's area intact, the person can still produce fluent speech, but without Wernicke's area the words chosen carry little meaning and understanding others is impaired. Slow, effortful speech with good comprehension is the prediction for damage to Broca's area.
